score_rationale: Strong commercial validation with at least 6 established database vendors actively selling K-12 educator contact lists for 15+ years: K12 Prospects (5M+ education contacts with 68 data points per contact covering 93,327 public schools, 26,583 private schools, 6,732 charter schools, 14,000 school districts, operating since 2010 with proprietary K12 Prospects Lab ranked #1 among competitors), K12 Data (4M+ educators by email offering 391 different K-12 education job titles including principal and superintendent), Education Data Lists (verified K-12 schools email database with principals, administrators, key decision-makers featuring emails, phone numbers, school/district details, GDPR-compliant and regularly updated), Emaillistus (verified K12 data for principals, superintendents, district staff across elementary/middle/high schools divided by private/charter/catholic segments), Principals-EmailList.com (5M+ contacts, 15+ years dedicated to creating high-quality verified school email lists), and ITNow Technologies (verified K-12 schools email database with principal/administrator names, emails, phones, job titles, school/district info, location details). All vendors emphasize data quality (GDPR/CAN-SPAM compliance, regular updates, customizable by region/school type/job role) and report serving EdTech companies, textbook publishers, and school suppliers for 10-15+ years, confirming sustained commercial demand. Four exceptionally high-value B2B buyer segments with massive LTV justification: (1) EdTech software and Student Information System (SIS) vendors (PowerSchool SIS serving 45M+ students at $5-$15/student/year for districts with 1,000-100,000 students = $5,000-$1,500,000/year contracts, Infinite Campus SIS at $3-$12/student, Skyward, Tyler Technologies Munis ERP, ClassLink single sign-on, Canvas/Schoology LMS platforms at $10,000-$500,000/year district-wide implementations, Renaissance Learning assessment tools, IXL adaptive learning subscriptions) selling mission-critical platforms where district contracts range $50,000-$5,000,000/year for large suburban and urban districts and customer lifetime value over 10-15 year retention cycles (extremely high switching costs due to historical student records migration, teacher training investment, parent portal dependencies) reaches $500,000-$75,000,000, making $149-$199 database deliver 2,500×-375,000× ROI when just two mid-size districts are closed; (2) Facilities, equipment, and infrastructure vendors (HVAC systems for school buildings at $500,000-$5,000,000 per district-wide upgrade across 10-50 school buildings, commercial playground equipment from Landscape Structures and GameTime at $50,000-$500,000 per elementary school installation, cafeteria equipment and commercial kitchen systems at $100,000-$1,000,000 per high school, security systems including metal detectors and surveillance cameras at $50,000-$500,000 per building, athletic facilities and gymnasium flooring at $200,000-$2,000,000, school bus fleet purchases at $100,000 per bus × 50-500 buses = $5M-$50M district fleet) where one district capital improvement contract = 250,000×-25,000,000× database cost ROI; (3) Textbook publishers and educational content providers (Pearson K-12 textbooks and digital curriculum, McGraw-Hill Education, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Scholastic literacy programs, with district adoptions ranging $500,000-$10,000,000 for K-12 math/ELA/science curriculum covering 5,000-50,000 students on 7-year adoption cycles typical in most states, plus digital supplemental materials from Discovery Education, BrainPOP, ReadWorks) where one large district adoption = 2,500×-50,000× database ROI; (4) Professional development and teacher training providers (NIET teacher evaluation systems, ASCD professional learning memberships at $500-$2,000 per educator × 500-5,000 teachers = $250,000-$10,000,000 district-wide contracts, Edutopia workshops, NCTM math training, district-wide PD consulting at $100,000-$2,000,000/year for ongoing coaching and implementation support) where one mid-size district PD contract = 500×-10,000× ROI. Total addressable market: NCES Common Core of Data reports 98,755 public schools (13,452 school districts) and 30,492 private schools as of 2024-25 school year, serving 50.8M public school students and 5.7M private school students, with K12 Prospects reporting 93,327 public schools + 26,583 private schools + 6,732 charter schools (many charter schools counted separately from traditional public) and 14,000 total districts including charter management organizations. Estimated 150,000-200,000 decision-maker contacts targeting principals, superintendents, assistant superintendents, curriculum directors, technology directors, business managers, facilities directors, and purchasing officers concentrated in suburban and urban districts with 1,000+ students (90% of total enrollment concentrated in 40% of districts per NCES data, creating high-value target segment of 5,000-6,000 large districts plus 25,000-30,000 individual schools). Public data is partially accessible via NCES and state education agencies: NCES Common Core of Data provides school name, address, phone, district affiliation, enrollment, and NCES ID for all public schools but does NOT include principal names or emails in bulk download (CCD Public School Name and Address File contains location/demographic data only, not administrator contacts), however many state Departments of Education publish school directories with principal names and contact information as part of transparency initiatives (Illinois ISBE Directories include entity name, administrator, address, contact information; other states vary in disclosure level). Engineering lift is moderate-to-high: download NCES CCD school/district directory files (free bulk CSV available annually), cross-reference with state DOE school directories across 50 states (some states publish CSV exports with principal emails, others require HTML scraping of individual school pages), scrape school district websites for administrator staff directories (most districts publish 'Staff Directory' or 'Administration' pages listing superintendent, assistant superintendents, principals, curriculum coordinators with direct emails/phones), enrich with third-party education databases (MDR Education providing similar data under commercial licensing, though expensive), normalize job titles across district-specific terminology (Principal vs Head of School vs Director, Superintendent vs District Administrator vs CEO in charter networks), deduplicate individuals holding multiple roles (small districts where one person serves as superintendent and principal), classify by school level (elementary, middle, high school, K-8, K-12), district size tier (small <1,000 students, medium 1,000-10,000, large 10,000-50,000, very large 50,000+ like NYC 1M, LA 600K, Chicago 350K), and district type (traditional public, charter, private, parochial, independent). No affordable flat-file competitor exists below $200 on Gumroad — all existing vendors (6+ identified, some operating 15+ years) use enterprise 'contact for quote' or Lab platform pricing with login-required access, typical patterns of $0.10-$0.40 per contact for quality education data = $5,000-$20,000 for 50,000-record targeted list (e.g., all high school principals in California or all superintendents in districts over 5,000 students), and subscription-based models requiring annual renewals for ongoing updates as principals/superintendents change positions frequently (average K-12 principal tenure only 4 years, superintendent tenure 5-6 years per NCES/AASA data requiring constant data refreshes). A $149-$199 one-time CSV would deliver 97-99% savings vs. enterprise per-contact pricing. Score is 7 (not 8) due to: (a) strong commercial demand validated by 6+ vendors operating 10-15+ years serving EdTech/publishers/suppliers, but less vendor density than insurance agents (7+ vendors) or property managers (7+ vendors), (b) exceptionally high buyer LTV across all four segments (EdTech software $500K-$75M lifetime, facilities/equipment $50K-$50M per project, textbook adoptions $500K-$10M per 7-year cycle, professional development $100K-$10M multi-year) where 1-2 customer acquisitions justify 2,500×-375,000× database investment making it among highest-ROI opportunities identified, (c) moderate TAM size (150K-200K decision-makers vs. 400K-1M for insurance agents or property managers, but concentrated in high-value large districts creates quality-over-quantity opportunity), (d) partial public data availability with moderate-to-high engineering complexity (NCES provides school location/enrollment data but NOT administrator contacts in bulk downloads, requiring state-by-state aggregation of DOE directories with inconsistent schemas plus extensive district website scraping to achieve comprehensive coverage — contrast with county assessor records for property managers where single county database contains all needed fields, or state insurance licensing where name/address/license in one lookup), (e) high data refresh requirements due to frequent principal/superintendent turnover (4-6 year average tenure means 15-25% of contacts become stale annually, though this creates ongoing resale opportunity for annual updated editions), and (f) extremely clear buyer pain points and validated demand (EdTech vendors MUST reach district technology directors and curriculum coordinators for software sales, textbook publishers target adoption committees before state deadlines, facilities vendors chase capital bond expenditures). Score not higher than 7 due to fragmented public data sources (no single federal database with administrator emails like IRS 990s for nonprofits, requiring 50-state DOE aggregation + 13,000+ district website scraping for comprehensive coverage vs. centralized public sources in higher-scoring opportunities) and need for annual updates to maintain quality (principal/superintendent turnover creates depreciation unlike property ownership or nonprofit board seats with longer tenure), though commercial demand and buyer LTV are among strongest identified (EdTech district contracts $50K-$5M justify massive prospecting spend, creating exceptional willingness-to-pay despite data complexity).
summary: A comprehensive CSV of all U.S. K-12 school principals, superintendents, and district administrators extracted from NCES Common Core of Data school/district directories, state Department of Education school directories across all 50 states, and district website staff directories. Each record includes administrator name and job title (Superintendent, Assistant Superintendent, Principal, Assistant Principal, Curriculum Director, Technology Director, Business Manager, Facilities Director, Purchasing Officer, Special Education Director), school/district name, school level (elementary, middle, high school, K-8, K-12), school type (traditional public, charter, private/independent, parochial), district size tier (enrollment: <1,000 students, 1,000-10,000, 10,000-50,000, 50,000+), address, city, state, ZIP, phone (main office and direct line where available), email (administrator direct email from district directories), district website, NCES school ID, NCES district ID, student enrollment, and free/reduced lunch percentage (proxy for Title I funding eligibility and district purchasing power). As of 2024-25 school year, NCES reports 98,755 public schools across 13,452 school districts serving 50.8M students, plus 30,492 private schools serving 5.7M students. K12 Prospects data shows 93,327 public schools + 26,583 private schools + 6,732 charter schools (charter schools sometimes counted within public school totals, sometimes separate) + 14,000 total districts/charter management organizations. Target output: 150,000-200,000 decision-maker contact records prioritizing high-value large districts (1,000+ students capturing 90% of total enrollment concentrated in top 40% of districts per NCES data = 5,000-6,000 large districts × 10-30 administrator contacts per district + 25,000-30,000 individual school principals). Concentrated in high-enrollment states: California (10,315 public schools, 1,037 districts, 6.2M students), Texas (9,025 schools, 1,023 districts, 5.4M students), Florida (4,309 schools, 74 large county districts, 2.9M students), New York (4,792 schools, 731 districts, 2.6M students), Illinois, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan. Four exceptionally high-value B2B buyer segments: (1) EdTech software and Student Information System vendors (PowerSchool SIS $5-$15/student/year for 1,000-100,000 student districts = $5,000-$1,500,000/year contracts, Infinite Campus $3-$12/student, Skyward, Tyler Munis ERP, ClassLink SSO, Canvas/Schoology LMS $10K-$500K/year, Renaissance Learning, IXL adaptive learning) where 10-15 year customer lifetime value = $500,000-$75,000,000 for large urban/suburban districts, making two mid-size district wins deliver 2,500×-375,000× database ROI; (2) Facilities and infrastructure vendors (district-wide HVAC upgrades $500K-$5M across 10-50 buildings, playground equipment $50K-$500K per elementary school, cafeteria/commercial kitchen systems $100K-$1M per high school, security systems $50K-$500K per building, athletic facilities $200K-$2M, school bus fleet $5M-$50M for 50-500 buses) where one capital project = 250,000×-25,000,000× ROI; (3) Textbook publishers (Pearson, McGraw-Hill, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Scholastic K-12 curriculum adoptions $500K-$10M per district for math/ELA/science on 7-year adoption cycles covering 5,000-50,000 students) where large district adoption = 2,500×-50,000× ROI; (4) Professional development providers (NIET teacher evaluation, ASCD memberships $500-$2K/educator × 500-5,000 teachers = $250K-$10M district-wide, ongoing PD consulting $100K-$2M/year) where mid-size district = 500×-10,000× ROI. A one-time $149-$199 CSV delivers 97-99% savings vs. traditional EdTech vendors charging $0.10-$0.40/contact ($5,000-$20,000 for 50K targeted records), with instant download vs. quote-required Lab platforms, providing complete K-12 administrator TAM for EdTech software, facilities vendors, textbook publishers, and professional development providers.

data_wanted: NCES (National Center for Education Statistics) Common Core of Data (CCD) provides comprehensive school and district directory information via annual bulk CSV downloads at nces.ed.gov/ccd/ccddata.asp: CCD Public School Name and Address File contains all 98,755 public schools (as of 2024-25) with fields including NCES school ID, school name, street address, city, state, ZIP, phone, school level (elementary, middle, high, K-8, K-12, other), school type (regular, special education, vocational, alternative), operational status (open, closed, future), enrollment by grade, free/reduced lunch eligible students (Title I indicator), locale code (city, suburban, town, rural), district NCES ID, district name; CCD School District Name and Address File contains 13,452 districts with district name, mailing address, phone, superintendent name (in some years), enrollment, locale, operational status. IMPORTANT: NCES CCD does NOT include principal names or administrator email addresses in bulk downloads — these must be supplemented from state sources. State Department of Education school directories (50 states publish varying levels of detail): Illinois State Board of Education ISBE Directories (isbe.net/pages/data-analysis-directories.aspx) include entity name, administrator name, address, contact information for all schools and districts; California CDE publishes school directory with principal names; Texas TEA school directory; Florida DOE school contact info; New York State Education Department school reports — each state has different schema and disclosure policies, with some states publishing CSV exports of administrator contacts while others require HTML scraping of individual school profile pages. District website staff directories: nearly all 13,452 school districts maintain 'Staff Directory' or 'Administration' pages on official websites listing superintendent, assistant superintendents for curriculum/business/operations, principals by school, department heads with direct email (firstname.lastname@districtname.org standard format) and office phone numbers — scraping 13,000+ district websites captures comprehensive administrator contacts not available in NCES or many state databases. MDR Education (commercial vendor) maintains similar K-12 administrator database via annual surveys and public records aggregation but requires expensive licensing ($10K+ per year typical), not suitable for DataStructured bootstrap model. Target fields per record: Administrator name (first, middle, last), job title (normalize across: Superintendent vs District Administrator vs CEO in charter networks, Assistant Superintendent for Curriculum & Instruction vs Chief Academic Officer, Principal vs Head of School vs Director, Assistant Principal vs Dean of Students, Technology Director vs CTO vs Director of Information Systems, Business Manager vs CFO, Facilities Director, Purchasing Officer/Procurement, Special Education Director, Curriculum Coordinator, Athletic Director), school name (if building-level administrator), district name, school level (elementary, middle, high, K-8, K-12), school type (traditional public, public charter, private independent, Catholic/parochial, other religious), district size tier by enrollment (<1,000 students small rural, 1,000-5,000 small suburban, 5,000-10,000 medium, 10,000-25,000 large suburban, 25,000-50,000 very large, 50,000+ urban mega-districts like NYC 1M, LA 600K, Chicago 350K), street address, city, state, ZIP, main office phone, administrator direct phone (where available), administrator direct email (from district directory or standardized firstname.lastname@district format validated via email verification API), district website URL, school website URL (if applicable), NCES school ID (for cross-reference with CCD enrollment/demographics), NCES district ID, student enrollment (school-level and district-level), free/reduced lunch percentage (0-100% as proxy for Title I funding eligibility and socioeconomic status — wealthier districts have lower percentages and larger discretionary budgets for EdTech/curriculum, while high-poverty Title I districts have dedicated federal funding for instructional technology), locale classification (city, suburban, town, rural), and state (for targeting by geography). Focus on high-value decision-makers: superintendents and assistant superintendents (district-level purchasing authority for SIS, curriculum, professional development), principals and assistant principals (building-level discretionary budgets for supplemental materials, input on district technology committees), technology directors (primary buyer for EdTech platforms, SIS selection, device procurement), curriculum directors and instructional coordinators (textbook adoption leaders, professional development planners), business managers and purchasing officers (RFP processes, vendor management, capital budget allocation). Estimated 150,000-200,000 total contacts: 13,452 districts × 5-10 district-level administrators (superintendent, asst supers for curriculum/business/operations/special ed, tech director, purchasing) = 65,000-135,000 district contacts + 100,000 public schools × 1.5 average contacts per school (principal, asst principal for schools over 500 students) = 150,000 building contacts, minus overlap where small district superintendent also serves as principal = 150K-200K unique decision-makers. Prioritize large districts: top 6,000 districts with 1,000+ students enroll 90% of all public school students per NCES data, so these 40% of districts represent majority of purchasing power — 6,000 large districts × 15-30 administrators per district (larger districts have more specialized roles: separate asst supers for elementary/secondary, multiple curriculum coordinators by content area, facilities directors, HR directors) = 90,000-180,000 high-value contacts in largest target segment. Data is partially public: NCES CCD school/district directories are federally funded public datasets with free bulk CSV downloads updated annually, many state DOE websites publish school directories with administrator names under transparency/open data initiatives, district websites publish staff directories for parent/community contact purposes — however no single centralized source contains administrator emails in bulk format (contrast with IRS 990s for nonprofits or state insurance licensing databases), requiring multi-source aggregation: NCES for school metadata (location, enrollment, demographics) + state DOE directories (administrator names, some emails) + district website scraping (comprehensive email/phone directory pages) to build complete dataset.

willingness_to_pay.signal: Four buyer segments with exceptional LTV and confirmed commercial demand (6+ vendors operating 10-15+ years serving EdTech market, K12 Prospects since 2010 ranked #1 platform): (1) EdTech software/SIS: District contracts $50K-$5M/year (PowerSchool for 10,000-100,000 student districts) generate $500K-$75M lifetime value over 10-15 year retention due to extreme switching costs (historical student data migration costs $500K-$5M in services, teacher training investment, parent portal adoption lock-in, state reporting integrations make SIS replacement equivalent to ERP migration). One mid-size district (20,000 students) paying $200K/year SIS fees = $2M over 10 years = 10,000× database cost. Two district wins = 20,000× ROI. EdTech vendors face 12-24 month sales cycles requiring RFP responses, superintendent/board presentations, pilot programs — they pay premium prices for high-quality decision-maker contacts to shorten sales cycles and increase win rates. (2) Facilities/infrastructure: District capital bond projects $5M-$50M (HVAC upgrades across 20 buildings, school bus fleet replacement, cafeteria modernization, security systems) where one district = 25,000×-250,000× database ROI. Facilities vendors (Trane HVAC, Blue Bird buses, Landscape Structures playgrounds) chase 5-10 year capital improvement cycles tied to voter-approved bond measures — they must identify districts with recently passed bonds (public info via state DOE bond calendars) and reach facilities directors and business managers before RFP issuance. Large projects justify $50K-$500K in engineering/design costs during pre-sales, making $149-$199 database negligible. (3) Textbook publishers: Large district adoptions $500K-$10M per 7-year cycle (Pearson math/ELA/science curriculum for 25,000 students across K-12) where one district = 2,500×-50,000× ROI. Publishers face state adoption calendars (Texas, California, Florida mega-adoptions every 7 years drive national market) and must reach curriculum directors 18-24 months before adoption deadlines for pilot programs and committee presentations. Missing one adoption deadline means waiting 7 years for next opportunity, creating urgent need for complete administrator contacts and willingness to pay premium for quality data. Traditional education list brokers charge $0.10-$0.40/contact ($5K-$20K for 50K records) with subscription renewals — publishers pay because stakes are so high ($10M adoption justifies $50K in marketing/sales spend). (4) Professional development: Multi-year PD contracts $250K-$10M for district-wide teacher training (NIET coaching for 2,000 teachers over 3 years = $4M contract) where one district = 1,250×-50,000× database cost. PD providers compete for Title II federal funds (dedicated to teacher quality) and state/local PD budgets, requiring relationships with superintendents and assistant superintendents for curriculum. All vendors operate subscription/quote-required models (K12 Prospects Lab requires login/quote, K12 Data contact for pricing, Education Data Lists custom quotes), confirming B2B buyers accept enterprise pricing for quality education data. No transparent flat-file pricing found below $200 on Gumroad. Opportunity to deliver instant-download CSV at $149-$199 (97-99% below $5K-$20K enterprise per-contact pricing) creates unprecedented value for EdTech/publishers/facilities vendors where single deal = $50K-$75M lifetime value and database cost is rounding error vs. total CAC (customer acquisition cost for EdTech district sale typically $50K-$500K including RFP responses, demos, pilot programs, travel to board meetings).
